title: Tuskegee Airmen: American Heroes
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Tuskegee Airmen, the African American pilots trained during World War II at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. The episode starts with the history of Black Americans in the military (Revolutionary War, War of 1812, Buffalo Soldiers, Harlem Hellfighters) and the 1925 Army War College study. It covers early Black aviators such as Alfred Anderson, Bessie Coleman, and James Banning and Thomas Allen, the Civilian Pilot Training Program, and the Double V campaign. Eleanor Roosevelt's flight with Anderson helped launch the Tuskegee training program. The hosts describe Colonel Noel Parrish and Benjamin O'Davis Jr., the ninety-nine Pursuit Squadron, and the harsh standards and washouts. They cover the Time magazine "cowardice" story, the January 1943 Sicily-area dogfight, bomber escort missions and the Red Tails nickname, the bomber-loss myth versus reality, and the postwar return home. They close with Truman's end of military segregation, O'Davis's later career, the Freeman Field Mutiny, and a listener mail segment about tit birds' social networks.
topics: Time magazine Tuskegee Airmen cowardice story

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the Tuskegee Airmen
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the Black History Month episode on the Tuskegee Airmen and briefly discuss the 2019-era films about them, including the HBO movie and Red Tails.

segments.title: African Americans in the military before World War II
segments.summary: The hosts review Black military service from the Revolutionary War and War of 1812 through Buffalo Soldiers and the Harlem Hellfighters, and describe the 1925 Army War College study that questioned Black soldiers' fitness.

segments.title: Early Black aviators and the Tuskegee program roots
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Army Air Corps as prestigious, the Tuskegee Institute's flight role, and early Black pilots like Alfred Anderson, Bessie Coleman, and James Banning and Thomas Allen. They explain how the black press spread these stories and how the Civilian Pilot Training Program got started.

segments.title: Double V campaign and Eleanor Roosevelt's flight
segments.summary: The Double V campaign for victory abroad and at home is described. Eleanor Roosevelt visits Moton Field and flies with Alfred Anderson, then urges her husband to push the program forward, though the timing is unclear.

segments.title: Founding of the segregated training program and the lawsuit
segments.summary: The program's early setup with the Army Air Corps and the Steerman trainers is described. Earlier rejections, the NAACP lawsuit filed by Yancey Williams, and the military's response of a segregated program with few cadets are covered.

segments.title: Life at Tuskegee: Jim Crow, Colonel Parrish, and the ninety-nine Squadron
segments.summary: Hosts describe hostility from white townspeople, the disarming of military police, Major James Ellison's removal, and Colonel Noel Parrish's fair training. They also cover the ninety-nine Pursuit Squadron and ground crews including Chief Alfred Anderson.

segments.title: Benjamin O. Davis Jr., training standards, and the first graduates
segments.summary: Davis's background at West Point and his role leading the ninety-nine squadron are covered, along with the high standards and washouts. The hosts describe the pressure on trainees and early praise from Secretary of War Stimson and Major General James Chaney.

segments.title: Overseas deployment, Pantelleria, and the Time magazine cowardice story
segments.summary: The squadron's delayed deployment to North Africa in 1943 is covered, along with dive-bombing missions that helped take Pantelleria. A Time magazine story questioned their bravery and kill count, which led Davis to be called to Washington.

segments.title: January dogfight, bomber escorts, and Red Tails
segments.summary: A January dogfight with German fighters yielded five kills with no losses. The 332nd Fighter Group was formed under Davis, who emphasized bomber escort duty. They flew P-51 Mustangs and painted their tails red, earning the Red Tails name.

segments.title: Bomber loss myth and postwar legacy
segments.summary: The hosts explain the myth that the Tuskegee Airmen never lost a bomber, from a Chicago Defender story, and the Air Force's later correction. They describe the return home without equality, Truman ending military segregation, Davis's later career, and the Freeman Field Mutiny.

segments.title: Listener mail on tit birds and social networks
segments.summary: A listener shares an Audubon magazine article about a British long-running study showing tit birds form social groups and appear to have friendships.

segments.title: Sign-off and resources
segments.summary: The hosts suggest documentaries and places to learn more, mention social media and email contact, and sign off.
